content.thinking:
I'm thinking through how to model the weapon as a plain object displayed touching the floor—on a stand or lying down—and wondering whether it still needs a root joint even without moving parts, so I should check a sample build for a plain object.

For the design, I'm settling on a large two-handed frost-forged battle axe with LoL-style exaggerated, dynamic shapes and glowing magic effects, readable from a high top-down camera. I'm picking a palette of deep navy shaft, pale frost steel, saturated cyan glow, and warm gold trim, and sizing the axe at roughly 1.5 meters, deciding to display it lying flat on a plinth for readability.

I'm reconsidering the display orientation, opting instead for the axe standing upright planted in a rocky frost base with ice crystals and snow, about 1.6 meters tall and 0.7 meters diameter, with the blade in the XY plane so the front view captures its silhouette. For the head shape, I'm going with a dramatic asymmetric design: a large crescent blade with extended horn tips on one side balanced by a smaller counter-blade on the other.

Working out the overall proportions: total height around 1.55 meters, plinth 0.12 meters, haft running up to the head centered near 1.25 meters, with a chunky main blade roughly 0.55 meters tall and 0.45 meters wide for an exaggerated, oversized feel.

Designing the plinth piece now—an octagonal stone base with stepped sides, topped with snow and surrounded by faceted ice crystal spikes.

Now I'm figuring out the haft: a dark indigo wood-grain shaft wrapped in leather grip bands with a glowing cyan rune inlay, plus a spiral leather cord wrap around the grip section using a helical sweep path. For the bottom, I'm placing a pommel cap with a faceted ice-crystal gem resting where the haft meets the plinth top.

Then I'm sketching the head assembly: a lathe-turned steel-and-gold collar at the haft's midpoint, from which I'm extruding the main blade. I'm plotting the crescent-shaped blade outline point by point in local coordinates, aiming for a convex cutting edge with flaring horn tips top and bottom for an elegant bearded-axe silhouette.

Then I'm reconsidering the scale — a 0.56m wide blade feels too chunky compared to real battle axes, so I decide to shrink the whole outline by a 0.75 factor to keep proportions believable while still stylized, and I'm starting to plan cutout details inside the blade.

Since true holes aren't supported in extrusion, I switch to layering plates instead — a pale steel base, a darker inlaid plate with glowing cyan runes, and a lighter beveled edge strip for the sharpened look, figuring out how to paint the edge brightness using coordinate-based distance calculations.

Checking the front face normal against the light direction, it comes out lit at around 0.5 while the back face falls into shadow, so cel shading would paint each flat face as one uniform tone.

But that feels too plain, so I'm layering in paint patterns keyed to surface coordinates: banding, gradients, and frost-like mottling for an icy, hand-painted look reminiscent of LoL splash art. I'm thinking through paint functions that create a pale-to-bright gradient based on distance from the blade's axis, plus a hard-edged diagonal highlight streak and crystalline frost cracking.

Now I'm working out the geometry: the bevel parameter handles the chamfered edge nicely, but the blade's thickness tapering is trickier since I want it to taper toward the edge along x while extrusion only tapers along y, so I'm reconsidering how to orient the outline axes to get the taper direction I actually want.

I'll cap the bevel so it shrinks to fit, keeping it small at 0.003, and let the faces stay flat with the planar taper. The outline runs from the haft side at lowest u to the edge at highest u, and now I want to add raised inlay plate details on the blade faces.

Simplifying: instead of tapering, I'll use a constant blade thickness with a beveled rim that chamfers inward to mimic a sharpened edge, then layer thin inlay plates on both faces with distinct colors and glowing rune lines for detail.

Now I'm positioning those inlay plates symmetrically on either side of the blade so they sit partially embedded, mirroring the design front-to-back. For the counter-blade on the other side, I'm thinking of a smaller, spikier "frost wing" shape with a few swept ice-shard points.

I'll make the two blades asymmetric: the main side a big crescent, the secondary side a smaller serrated fin topped with a point, looping through both orientations to create different outlines. I'm also planning a faceted spear-tip spike on top of the haft, extending the overall height upward.

Now I'm working out proportions: haft from the plinth top up to the socket, blade centered around that socket spanning roughly 0.97–1.59m, and a tapered four-sided pyramid spike crowning the top to total around 1.7m, with the plinth kept wide for stability.

For the spearhead itself I'm leaning toward a single leaf-shaped extruded plane with a tapered thickness and central ridge, pale icy color with a glowing rune, rather than a cruciform design. Around the socket I'm adding clusters of three faceted hexagonal ice crystals on the front and back sides, angled diagonally outward, built from six-sided cylinder/cone prisms.

I'm deciding which parts glow and which stay flat: crystals, blade runes, the socket gem, pommel gem, and edge lines get the cyan glow colors while the rest use plain cel-shaded ice tones. To keep the part count manageable I'm writing a small helper that batches same-colored small geometries like rivets, studs, icicles, and wraps into a single bag, then merges them into one mesh attached to the root bone at the end.

All my primitive geometries already share indexed position/normal/uv attributes so merging should work fine with flat coloring. I'm also thinking about adding a couple extra joints for moving parts -- a hanging frost charm pendant on a cord and cloth tassel strips swinging from the haft -- deciding whether to treat them as hinge or tail-type roles.

For the pendant, I'll build a short three-link chain with a sweep-tube cord and a crystal piece riding on the tip bone, plus two tassel cords on their own chains. Now shifting to the overall painting style -- going for that League of Legends hand-painted look with strong gradients, saturated color banding, and pale blue-white steel with hard highlights for the metal parts.

Setting the palette: deep navy for shadows, cool steel blues with icy light tones, a vivid cyan glow with a near-white core, and warm gold for contrast, with a dark purple-leather accent to round it out. Keeping the flat color count to 64 and not counting paint gradients toward that limit.

For shading, I'm planning to use a two-tone cel-shading approach on turned shapes like the haft and collars since the varied surface normals make that style read nicely. I'm weighing texel density for the paint sheet against total painted area — leaning toward a 2048 paint texture size for crisper rune details despite the extra cost, starting at 1024 to check before bumping up.

For the double-bit blade's main paint, I'm designing a banded gradient from dark steel-blue near the haft out to icy white at the edge using hard cel-like steps, with frost-crack lines and a diagonal white highlight streak layered on top — though I need to account for how the crescent-shaped edge distorts where those bands should fall relative to the outward distance coordinate.

Instead of relying purely on the outward distance, I'm computing the actual edge profile by scanning the outline polyline for the maximum outward distance at each height, then measuring distance inward from that true edge to assign the colored bands, which better follows the crescent shape. The tricky part is handling the horn tips, where the outward distance behaves unpredictably near the near-horizontal edges.

This uniform rim distance treats cutting edge and top edges the same, but the bit's root edges near the haft shouldn't glow as bright as the actual cutting edge—I need to distinguish those regions.

For the curve smoothing, I'll go with zero smoothing and sample enough points along the crescent's curves to approximate a faceted, low-poly look while still reading as flowing. I'll build the outline by sampling points along bezier curves manually in code rather than relying on automatic smoothing.

For the inlay, I'm thinking of using the outline's own coordinates directly as paint distance input rather than scaling, then defining distance bands (bright steel rim, mid zone, deeper base) plus a smaller inset raised panel carrying glowing rune details, handled through the same multi-band paint logic.

I also want geometric raised features — a central ridge rod from the collar outward and engraved lines — along with a frost-forged aesthetic: icicle spikes near the horn and crystal shards jutting outward on the blade's back facets. For the glowing runes, I'll texture a transparent decal plane positioned just off the blade face, drawn as an SVG with a flowing frost motif of snowflake shapes and curved lines following the blade's crescent.

Now I'm working out the decal plane's size and orientation — matching its dimensions to the blade region and figuring out how the drawing's coordinate axes map to world space depending on which face (+Z or -Z) it's applied to, since the back face needs a mirrored version of the artwork to read correctly.

I'm mapping the decal plane coordinates to a pixel-based SVG viewBox, then sketching glowing elements: an inset crescent line tracing the blade edge with rune-like ticks along it, plus a snowflake motif near the root.

For the glow effect, I'll layer a brighter narrow core stroke over a wider colored stroke, keeping in mind cards get cut away at low alpha so no extra halo is needed. For the inset curve itself, I'll compute it by scaling the outline polygon inward toward the blade's interior centroid rather than doing per-vertex normal offsets.

This gives a nonuniform inset that works nicely with the crescent shape, with the horn tips getting pulled in more dramatically. I'll build the inner outline as a glowing cyan stroke, add short rune-like tick marks along the cutting edge, and place a small six-branch frost snowflake near the base.

Now I'm sketching out the piece list: the plinth needs a lathed octagonal profile with stepped radii and a chamfered top, painted as navy stone with frost mottling and snow highlights on upward-facing surfaces, plus a glowing rune ring engraved into the top.

I'm planning glowing rune decals on the plinth's eight side faces, each using the same glyph texture oriented outward, and then surrounding ice shard clusters at the base using hexagonal prisms with cone tips in flat cel-shaded cyan tones, possibly with a glowing core inside each shard.

I'm adding frost crust details with flattened white sphere "snow" blobs along the plinth edges, then moving to the haft design: a straight tapered tube with faceted cel shading in deep indigo with lighter grain streaks, considering torus rings or helix sweeps for the leather wrap section near the base.

For the grip, I'm working out a cord-wrapped helix in pale cyan-white spiraling over dark leather, calculating turn counts and triangle budgets to keep the geometry manageable, and now thinking about ways to simplify the approach further.

Rather than fully modeling the helix I could paint diagonal wrap stripes onto the haft using spiral paint coordinates, combining a geometric helix for the grip with painted texture elsewhere. For the pommel, I'm planning a lathed dark-steel cap widening near the bottom with gold bands and a hex gem, positioning it to rest just above the snow near the plinth top.

The pommel butt will have a small spike sinking into the plinth for a planted look, with a tiny crystal gem shape below for an icy, fragile accent. For the axe head, I'm considering a lathed octagonal socket with flared gold-ringed ends and a central bulge where the blade plates insert, treating it as a solid block form the blade extrudes pass through rather than separate pieces.

Now I'm planning the blades themselves: main and secondary edges with glowing inlay decals on both faces, gold rivet studs near the socket root, and painted engraving details. I want to add frost crystal clusters built from merged cylinder-and-cone shapes oriented along a direction vector, clinging to the blade spine and root, plus a leaf-shaped ice-shard spearhead tip with a tapering center ridge.

For the top, I'm adding a glowing cyan slit down the ridge, a gold collar, and small curved frost-horn prongs swept outward like a crown at the spearhead's base for extra silhouette flair. Then I'm sketching a pendant charm hanging from a jointed chain near the secondary blade's root, plus cloth tassels at the haft collar for added movement.

Writing ribbon sweep code...

I'm adding gold studs and rivets to the socket rings, plinth corners, and blade root plates, plus gold cuff plates around the socket and a thin spine fuller ridge running along the blade's center for extra engraved detail.

Next I'm defining a golden langet shape — small trapezoidal cap plates at the blade root attached to the socket, with thicker geometry and gold-cel coloring. Then I'm moving on to the secondary blade's icicle-tooth spikes along its back edge, mapping out the outline coordinates for a smaller fin shape.

Still plotting fang coordinates...

Still defining fang outline points...

Still plotting crescent coordinates...

Checking the overall proportions, the blade span looks too large relative to the haft length, so I'm scaling the blade outline down by about 0.88 to bring the total weapon height closer to a realistic 1.8m for a two-handed polearm axe.

I'm also placing a faceted gem at the socket junction, using an elongated octahedron shape set in a gold bezel ring to act as a glowing focal point on the weapon.

Thinking about readability from a top-down camera, I decide the axe should stay upright with a wide crescent blade for a clear silhouette, rather than tilting it—now moving on to coding the blade's glowing rune details.

Writing blade paint function...

Still defining color bands and ridge lines...

For face shading, I'll quantize noise into discrete toon-style levels and apply cel shading based on surface normal direction relative to the light, darkening the back face since its dot product with the light falls into shadow range.

I decide to skip cel-shading on the blade faces themselves, letting the standard material's real lighting handle them, while still applying cel treatment to the beveled outline for a hand-painted feel. Now I'm moving on to building the crystal geometry directly.

Writing geometry setup code...

I realize I need to apply transform matrices to position, rotate, and scale each piece before merging, but I hit a snag: three.js's polyhedron geometries like octahedrons are non-indexed while cylinders and boxes are indexed, so mixing them will break the merge function unless I convert them all to a consistent format first.

Merged parts attach to the root joint while hanging charm pieces attach to their own charm joints. For crystal shapes, I'm combining a hexagonal prism with a cone tip to form a pointed shard, then orienting it with a quaternion rotation from the default up-axis to whatever direction it needs to point, and positioning its base accordingly. Now I'm working out clusters of small frost crystals growing outward from the blade faces near the root, varying their sizes and tilt angles for a natural jagged look.

I'm picking a color palette for the crystals -- a glowing cyan for the light-emitting ones, and a few cooler pale blues and deeper blue tones for the rest. Now I'm planning rune decal textures for the blade faces using flat plane geometry with a glow effect layered on top, and working out the UV-to-pixel mapping so the SVG texture aligns correctly with each blade's actual dimensions in meters.

Working through the raster sizing and texture atlas budget -- settling on 768px textures per face to keep stroke widths crisp while fitting within a 4096 atlas, and figuring out how to mirror the texture for the opposite-facing blade surface so the runes read correctly from both sides.

So I'll add a flip parameter to the SVG generator that mirrors the x-coordinate mapping when needed for the back-facing drawing. Then for the secondary blade on the model's right, viewed from the front face, the drawing's right side corresponds to world +X, so the blade extends accordingly.

I'm defining a mapX function that converts world x-coordinates to pixel positions, flipping sign depending on whether it's the front or back face. Now I'm starting to lay out the inlay SVG content for the main blade, beginning with a scaled polygon for the inner glowing outline.

Writing polygon inset logic...

I'm also planning glow rune lines at specific inset distances with tick marks between them, plus a central snowflake, and a procedural "frost fern" motif—a trunk line branching diagonally from the blade root with shrinking side branches to mimic radiating frost crystals.

Now I'm working out the stroke colors and widths for the SVG—an outer cyan halo and inner near-white core—checking that scaling to final texture resolution keeps the thin core line visible rather than lost to anti-aliasing. I'm also tallying texture counts: separate atlases for blade front/back and secondary decal front/back, sized to stay within a 4096 atlas budget.

I'm deciding on small 128px rune decal textures for the plinth faces, and thinking through which parts get painted (plinth, haft, socket, blades, spearhead, ribbons) without overdoing it. For top-down readability I want a glowing rune ring on the plinth top plus a visible cross-section, and I'm placing ice crystals right at the plinth base near floor level. I'm now defining the octagonal lathe profile for the plinth with specific radius/height points and an 8-segment spin rotated 22.5° so a flat face points forward.

Still refining lathe points...

I'm planning a helix wrap along the grip with gold ring bands above and below, a flared ice-cluster collar under the spearhead, and a socket leading up to the spear tip. I'm also adding hanging ribbons attached via a small gold torus ring near the socket base.

Still designing ribbon geometry...

For the pendant, I'm thinking of attaching a small frost charm on a cord hanging from the bottom horn tip of the main blade, dropping down roughly 0.12 units.

I'm calculating the exact horn tip position using the outline coordinates scaled down, which places it near (0.30, 0.88) in world space. From there I'll drop a cord with a small gold torus ring at the top where it meets the horn, keeping the ring thin so it reads as attached to the thin blade edge.

I'll place the ring at the horn's bottom edge, with the loop in the YZ plane threading around the horn's thickness and spanning vertically past its edge—I'll preview and adjust positioning. Given the time constraints, I should just write the full file now, setting up a deterministic RNG for the crystal arrangement and helper functions for orienting geometry and generating crystal shapes.

Writing crystal geometry function...

I'm converting each geometry piece to non-indexed before merging to keep attributes consistent, and adding random spin rotation to crystals for facet variation. I'm also setting up the crystal-adding function with bag keys tracking color and a glow flag for luminous crystals.

Now I'm working through part flushing with flat color material and planning out the painted parts list, starting with the plinth stone texture that blends snow on top surfaces with chiseled navy-stone blocks below using layered hex color scales.

Writing the frost edge zigzag logic...

Figuring out paint for the socket and gold trim details, deciding to use flat gold cel shading for langets and reusing blade paint with outline for the spearhead, then thinking about adding a glow effect for the socket gem using a scaled octahedron.

Now I'm defining the geometry parameters for the socket, working out the lathe profile with radius and height coordinates that shape the waist and curves along the axis.

Still shaping the langet plates...

The spearhead tip at the top gets a leaf-shaped outline with a sharp point, tapered thickness along its length, ready for coloring.

Computing the taper interpolation for the glow rod's radius along its length, then thinking about adding small prong details at the spearhead base's crown.

Now I'm designing hanging icicles underneath the socket's bottom ring and surface crystal clusters near the blade root.

I'm scattering crystal clusters across the plinth's outer edge too, varying their size and glow, then adding a flattened snow mound and blobs around the base. Finally I'm planning a flat rune torus on the plinth top with a ring of small glowing rune boxes encircling it.

Now I'm placing eight outward-facing rune decal planes on the plinth's octagonal faces, working out the apothem radius and vertex angles so each decal centers correctly on a flat face rather than a corner.

I need a rune glyph texture, so I'll sketch a small SVG with a handful of hand-drawn runic path shapes in cyan, spaced across the viewbox. Then I'll move into defining the blade geometry with typed UV point arrays and a helper to convert them into outline points for the sharp/blunt edges.

Now I'm thinking through corner smoothing — I want sharp corners only at the blade tips, not rounded, while root corners might need subtler handling. Since default smoothing would round everything, I'm considering marking sharp points explicitly and possibly sampling curved segments manually through control points rather than relying on uniform smoothing.

I realize root corners near the socket are hidden anyway, so I can safely mark them sharp too. To keep my distance calculations consistent with the smoothed extrusion, I'll implement a matching Chaikin-style corner-cutting function that replaces unsharp corners with quarter-point pairs along neighboring edges, run for the same number of rounds as the extrude smoothing, so both representations stay aligned.

Now I'm writing the point-to-polygon distance helper and the blade paint function, which checks surface normal angle to distinguish bevel/wall faces from the main face, then uses the polygon distance to drive edge brightness based on proximity to the outline.

Still refining color bands...

Working out the coordinate mapping function...

Still writing SVG code...

Adding glow halos to the texture lines, setting texture size, then simplifying the secondary blade decal and spearhead glow. I'm placing gold rivet spheres at langet positions and starting to define the joint skeleton structure for ribbons and pendant pieces.

Now I'm building the ribbon chains using Catmull-Rom paths off the root joint, then sweeping box-section geometry along each chain to form the ribbon shape with sideways and normal half-extents.

I'm also setting up a dangling charm chain off the horn tip with its own short Catmull path, and sweeping a thin cord radius along it for the chain segments, with a crystal piece attached separately at the tip joint.

I'm building the crystal geometry as an elongated octahedron gem with glow, oriented downward from the attachment point, plus a gold cap ring using a torus for the mount.

I'll keep the facets flat so engine lighting handles the faceted shading naturally, matching that high-contrast stylized look. I'm also adding small extras like icicle drips and a radial frost bloom on the plinth top before writing out the final builder code with proper imports and glow effects.

Setting up imports and color palette constants...

I'll go with crimson ribbons and gold accents for contrast, wrapping the lower haft in crimson cord, and using a blue-toned grain texture for the haft paint. Now I'm setting up the build metadata and starting the builder function for the axe.

Setting up joints and geometry bags...

Writing placement helper logic...

Now I'm designing a cluster function that scatters crystals around a direction with jittered offsets and scaled sizes, and a ring function for tori that need their default z-axis geometry rotated before being aimed along an arbitrary direction.

Writing plinth and frost shader logic...

I'll shrink the mound so it sits as a small drift around the pommel instead of burying the rune rings, keeping those rings on the plinth top with their tick marks intact, then add a thin glowing torus ring around the base for extra shine.

Writing blade coordinates...

Verifying the tip angle looks sharp enough, then moving to designing the secondary fang set with three points, trying out coordinates for the top fang tip.

Still mapping fang geometry...

I'm adding gold rivets as small spheres positioned along the plate edges, then working out the decal plane offset so it sits just outside the bevel without clipping through the gold langet overlay.

Now I'm writing a helper function that converts polygon coordinates into SVG paths for the rune engravings, mapping the UV space onto pixel coordinates and handling face orientation and inset offsets.

Working out the inset math for edge insetting — computing orientation via signed area, finding inward normals for each edge, and using the miter formula with clamping to avoid blowups at sharp corners. I'm also figuring out how to place tick marks along the inset boundary using the smoothed vertex points.

I'm smoothing the polygon points with Chaikin's algorithm, subsampling every other vertex, then planning out a frost fern texture, a runestrip decal for the plinth, and the leaf-shaped spearhead outline before moving to the top prongs.

Now I'm shaping the collar lathe profile below the socket with a flared taper and gold trim torus at the top, then setting up a helical wrap spiral around the haft with its turn count, pitch, and sweep radius.

I'm sizing the crimson wrap in pentagon cross-section with 18 turns giving gaps of visible dark haft between coils, keeping the triangle count reasonable, then planning a thinner gold wrap near the upper grip with a tighter pitch as an accent.

I'll skip tassel loops for now but keep part counts moderate, adding gold inlay collars and a thin glowing spiral helix along the upper haft to suggest etched energy runes.

Now I'm setting up the ribbon geometry hanging from the gold ring near the top of the haft, using curved paths through a few control points on front and back. I'm reconsidering placement since ribbons draped directly in front at that width would obscure the haft too much, so I'm thinking about shifting them to hang from the sides instead.

Still writing ribbon paint logic...

Now I'm planning the socket's decorative details: a ring of small downward-pointing icicle cones beneath it, glowing gemstones on the bezel front and back, and a gold torus ring wrapped around the socket edge, positioning everything by radius and z-offset to fit snugly against the socket surface.

I'm also sketching in a few extra floating ice shard particles hovering near the blade tips for a bit of magical flair, keeping it minimal so it doesn't overcrowd the design.

Now I'm finalizing the build, double-checking the lathe outline closure and paint stops for the plinth and gem shapes before writing out the full file.

input.command: ls; ls samples | head -5; ls scratch 2>/dev/null | head
